newsitem.title: USA: Polish prince sues in U.S. to recover artwork.
newsitem.headline: Polish prince sues in U.S. to recover artwork.

text.p: A Polish prince has filed suit in Manhattan to recover an oil painting he says the Nazis stole from his family during the Second World War, his lawyer said on Friday.
The oil painting, by Dutch master Jan Mostaert is known as "Portrait of a Lady, presumably Anne of Bretagne." It reportedly is worth between $70,000 and $90,000.

The painting was put up for sale by Donald Turcotte, an Ithaca, N.Y. geophysicist who is a professor at Cornell University. He had consigned the painting to Sotheby's auction gallery for a scheduled January 1997 sale.
After Prince Adam Karol Czartoryski-Borbon became aware of the sale, his lawyer notified Sotheby's and sent them a letter and proof claiming ownership of the painting.

"Sotheby's is on the sideline, holding the painting in question and we are waiting for resolution of the dispute by the court and the parties involved," Kevin Bousquette, chief operating officer for the auction house said.

In papers filed in Manhattan Supreme Court late on Thursday, the Prince's attorney Steven Hammond said that at the time of the 1939 Nazi invasion of Poland, the painting was in the Goluchow collection that belonged to the prince's family. He is suing Turcotte to recover the painting.
When Czartoryski's uncle died in 1978, he inherited the estate, including the painting, the prince said in a telephone news conference held in his lawyer's Wall Street office.

Speaking from his home in London, Czartoryski, 57, who is the cousin of Juan Carlos, the King of Spain, said the painting had been in his family over 200 years. "All I know is that it was confiscated in January 1942 by the Nazis and held in the National Museum in Warsaw until it disappeared from circulation," said Czartoryski, a business consultant.
How the painting next turned up in a collection owned by the Archbishop of Salzburg in Austria, is a mystery.
"We have no information on how or whether the painting ever got into the hands of the Archbishop of Salzburg," Hammond said. A hearing on the matter is set for May 9.

But Robert Clune, the lawyer representing Turcotte said it was his understanding the painting came from the Archbishop's collection. He said they were "very surprised" when the Prince popped up to say the painting belonged to him.

The painting next surfaced when the M. Knoeder and Co. gallery sold it to Turcotte's mother in 1958. She gave it to her son in 1963. A spokeswoman for the gallery said they would have to check their files for documentation as to how the gallery obtained the painting.
